intro: Ten discoveries for your curiosity: retro machines, Linux tinkering, AI, strange mysteries, new science and Christian hope. Source pages and publication dates checked; older research and republished material are identified below.

items.title: GNOME: custom Quick Settings toggles and a new Newsflash beta
items.summary: This week's GNOME roundup covers script-driven Quick Settings buttons with dropdown menus, plus Newsflash 6.0 beta's improved article view, podcast playback and PDF export.
items.why: Your Fedora panel projects and RSS widget make both halves useful: ideas for desktop controls and a native reader worth exploring.

items.title: You Are Empty returns with a modernised Absolute Edition
items.summary: The 2006 alternate-history horror shooter has been revived with widescreen support, adjustable FOV, controller support and extensive fixes. GamingOnLinux lists the Windows release under Proton/Wine.
items.why: A collision of retro gaming, unsettling science and Soviet mystery could appeal to your taste for strange worlds, with a Linux angle for your gaming setup.

items.title: A homemade RISC-V processor powers a 32-game retro console
items.summary: Hackaday spotlights a custom FPGA console running DOOM, CP/M software and Chip-8 games. The builder documents the CPU, framebuffer, serial bandwidth limits and fixed-point raycasting.
items.why: This is your sort of first-principles rabbit hole: understanding the whole machine, from processor design to the pixels, rather than just installing an emulator.

items.title: A garage museum connects vintage computers to modern AI
items.summary: GeekWire tours Darko Mesaros's working collection, where a Commodore 64 and a 1984 DEC teletype become interfaces to modern coding agents and cloud tools.
items.why: It brings together your interest in old hardware, local AI and making machines do unexpected things. The repair stories are as appealing as the AI demonstrations.

items.title: AI software cloning and the fight to take back the internet
items.summary: ABC interviews developers using AI to reproduce familiar software features, including creative and office tools. It examines their ambitions, the quality concerns and the unresolved ownership questions.
items.why: After building your own desktop extensions and replacing tools that don't suit you, the idea of creating software around your own needs should resonate.

items.title: AJ Gentile: Earth's Strangest Mysteries and Wildest Conspiracy Theories
items.summary: The Why Files host joins Shawn Ryan for a 2-hour-43-minute conversation spanning Tesla and Tunguska, time-travel paradoxes, AI, surveillance and unusual historical claims. These are discussion topics and speculative claims, not established discoveries.
items.why: You specifically enjoy The Why Files, and this gives AJ room for a longer conversation. The AI chapter starts at 1:20:06 and the Tesla discussion at 48:40.
items.source: Shawn Ryan Show / The Why Files

items.title: A rose-coloured meteorite opens a window into ancient Mars
items.summary: NASA-funded researchers identify Teghaza 001 as exceptionally ancient Martian crust, with evidence of water alteration around 4.1 billion years ago. Its minerals provide clues to a region not previously represented by such a sample.
items.why: A good science mystery with a physical object at its centre: how researchers trace a desert stone to Mars and reconstruct its history from mineral fingerprints.

items.title: Quantum-battery research gets a closer look
items.summary: This October article revisits a March 2026 experiment combining light absorption and electrical extraction in a microcavity. The paper reports power scaling faster than device capacity; it remains an experimental demonstration, far from a practical storage battery.
items.why: Your solar-and-battery tinkering gives you a practical reason to care about energy research, while the collective quantum effect offers an intriguing physics rabbit hole.

items.title: On the third day he rose again: resurrection and new creation
items.summary: Andrew Davison explores Christ's bodily resurrection as the heart of the gospel and the beginning of creation's renewal, drawing on Scripture, early Christian writers and Aquinas.
items.why: It connects your interest in Aquinas and Christian hope with the question of what salvation and the renewal of creation actually mean.

items.title: Stay awake: living faithfully while awaiting Christ
items.summary: Republished on 29 October as part of a Lutheran series on the last things, Robert Smith's reflection considers spiritual watchfulness, the beauty of creation and continuing the work of love while awaiting Christ's return. The original text dates to 2018.
items.why: It speaks to your interest in Christ's return while linking watchfulness to everyday faithfulness, generosity and the person in front of you.
items.source: What Does This Mean? / Robert Smith
